items.title: Matthew Barney Nearly Directed a 29-Hour Opera Cycle But Declined: ‘I Don’t Think I Can Quit My Job for Two Years’
items.summary:
Matthew Barney, the artist behind epic film projects such as The Cremaster Cycle and River of Fundament , very nearly took on yet another gargantuan project. But he declined the opportunity, fearing the time commitment involved, according to a freshly published New York Magazine profile.

That project would have been an opera cycle by the German composer Karlheinz Stockhausen called Licht . Written between 1977 and 2003, Licht is composed of seven operas, one for each day of the week, and calls in parts for actual helicopters and what the New York Times once described as an “intergalactic camel.” The cycle was staged in its entirety for the second time ever at the Deutsche Oper Berlin earlier this year, while portions of it appeared at New York’s Park Avenue Armory in 2024.

Licht may seem like a natural fit for Barney, whose projects are characterized by extravagance, ambition, and their monumental scale. But he told New York ’s Zachary Woolfe that Licht required more time than he had. “I don’t think I can quit my job for two years,” he said .

Moreover, he signaled that he might done making projects so big as The Cremaster Cycle altogether. Widely debated and rarely shown in its entirety, that cycle is composed of five films loosely centered around the development of sexual organs in the embryo. The three-hour-long Cremaster 3 (2002)—a film that involves the Chrysler Building, the Guggenheim Museum, Richard Serra, mysterious rituals, and a memorable scene involving cars and bikes—appeared on ARTnews ’s list of the best artworks of the 21st century so far .

No longer, it…

items.title: The Body review – this sexy retro high school drama is like Cruel Intentions … with added Satanic rituals
items.summary:
This coming-of-age tale of Catholic school girls is gleefully camp from the off – and full of fun references to its 2004 setting. And then a Halloween party goes wrong…

What’s more judgmental than a teenage girl? Easy: the Catholic church. Deliciously, Netflix’s new YA drama The Body has both in equal measure. It’s Halloween 2004 at St Mark’s Catholic school and the social hierarchy is exactly as you would expect. Perched at the top is the dance troupe, the Lions, presided over by Anya (Kristina Bogic) and Elise (Sara Boustany), two best friends skirting around their sexual chemistry. The show’s resident outcasts are Lisbeth (Geena Meszaros) and Leo (Jackson Kelly), previously homeschooled siblings who live a limited existence with their unwell mother. Leo seems like a harmless weirdo (or do his disturbing drawings suggest otherwise?) while Lisbeth is a classic loser desperate to ingratiate herself with the cool crowd.

Her opportunity arises when she’s invited to a Halloween party at an abandoned convent nicknamed Devil’s House ... what could possibly go wrong? Dressed as “Slutty God” in an attempt to meet the raunchy dress code, Lisbeth heads to the party, where she’s disappointed to learn that a free spot on the Lions team has been filled by Grace (Sofia Wylie), the devout niece of the school’s priest. But when an ecstasy-fuelled, Satan-baiting initiation ritual leaves Grace comatose and the Lions experiencing hallucinations and seizures, the equilibrium of the school is upended.

Continue reading...

items.title: How Does an Artist Know When She’s Done? A Major Marisa Merz Retrospective Turns the Question on Its Head
items.summary:
Italian artist Marisa Merz (1926–2019) was famously camera-shy. In rare snapshots, such as a captivating photograph taken by Claudio Abate at her 1975 solo show in Rome, she would retreat from the camera’s gaze. Before Abate’s camera, Merz appears clad in her woven nylon Scarpette (Little Shoes) , 1968, her back to him as she gazes out an open window at the moon.

The turn away is emblematic of Merz’s artistic ethos writ large. As she once wrote, in a 1975 issue of Data Arte magazine, “The artist is already an established role, like the wife, the son. But I don’t go along with these roles.”

View of “Marisa Merz: The Dance of the Hours” at Galleria d’Arte Moderna e Contemporanea (GAM) Turn. 

Photo Giorgio Perottino 

Merz was the only woman affiliated with Arte Povera, a loose movement christened in 1967 by curator Germano Celant that rejected the commodification of art and celebrated presence and materiality through nontraditional media and process-based practices. Even within this iconoclast milieu, she remained an outlier, not only for her inscription of domestic labor into her work—in her 1967 film The Count , she is seen in her kitchen sorting beans—but also for her use of figuration from the 1970s onward. Her unruly aluminum installations, paraffin pools, and woven forms were overlooked in the 1960s and 1970s, but she has gained wider recognition in recent years. Since the 1990s, major exhibitions of her work have been staged across Europe and the US, and in 2013, the Venice Biennale honored her with a Golden Lion.

Marisa Merz: Living Sculpture , 1966. 

Photo Rolf…
items.t: How Does an Artist Know When She’s Done? A Major Marisa Merz Retrospective Turns the Question on Its Head

items.title: When Animals Were Put on Trial in Medieval Europe
items.summary:
Most of us twenty-first-century urbanites have a fairly sentimental view of farm animals, precisely because so many generations have gone by since they’ve been part of our daily lives. (In South Korea, where I live, the agricultural past remains just within living memory. Perhaps that’s why so many restaurants in Seoul advertise their meat with pictures of the animals it comes from, sometimes dressed in chef’s garb and cheerfully serving up the very dishes they’re about to become.) Things were different in medieval Europe, where animals were both a necessity and a potential danger. History records many instances of serious harm done to humans by horses, bulls, and especially pigs, who seem to have had a particular tendency to turn on children.

Today we would describe the killing of a child as an inhuman act, a term that, in these cases, applies more than figuratively. As for the fate of the violently offending animal, we might imagine that it would be summarily slaughtered, but between the tenth and eighteenth centuries — and especially in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries — it might well have been brought into a courtroom first. Though other creatures had already been subject to legal proceedings for quite some time, “the earliest recorded pig trial took place in Fontenay-aux-Roses, just outside Paris, in 1266,” writes Alexander Lee at History Today . “By the early fifteenth century, however, they had become established practice throughout Normandy and the Île-de-France,” eventually spreading beyond the border to Italy, Germany, and the Low Countries.

items.title: European Intellectual History Since Nietzsche: A Free Online Course from Yale
items.summary:
Taught by historian Marci Shore , “ European Intellectual History Since Nietzsche ” surveys the story of modern thought, from the late 18th century to the late 20th.

Along the way, the course explores major trends in modern European thought: Marxism-Leninism, psychoanalysis, expressionism, structuralism, phenomenology, existentialism, anti-politics, and deconstruction. Intellectual figures covered in the course include Nietzsche, Lenin, Kafka, Freud, Husserl, de Beauvoir, Heidegger, Arendt, Adorno, Sartre, Girard, Foucault, Derrida, and Havel.

items.title: Heartland review – Jessica Chastain’s Netflix country music thriller is more miss than hit
items.summary:
The Oscar winner plays a singer turned detective searching for her niece in an overly generic Nashville-based mystery that fails to find its footing

Given the popularity of its music and the streaming services’ interest in faith-based programming, I’m always a little surprised that there aren’t more movies and TV shows about Nashville. Well, at least the idea of Nashville, the country music mecca that is perpetually struggling to define itself within and against the country at large, a place that has always been more diverse than its reputation yet still stands for a certain image of white, Christian Americana. There are plenty of enduring contradictions to mine there – the hyper-masculine men singing with their hearts on their sleeve, the Madonna-badass complex among its relatively few female stars, the suburban money in a genre ostensibly speaking to the rural common man.

Netflix seems to be aiming for some of those complexities with Heartland, a patchy neo-noir thriller starring Jessica Chastain as a washed-up former star turned vigilante detective with an axe to grind on Music Row. Chastain’s Misty Jones is certainly a thorny Nashville archetype, a female lead we might call “unlikable” painted in the stark terms of a bad country song (said with love as someone raised on country radio). The first five minutes of the nearly two-hour feature from Shana Feste, the writer-director perhaps best known for the 2010 movie Country Strong that launched Gwyneth Paltrow’s brief singing career , churn through the greatest hits of on-screen female fuck-up: teary loneliness,…
items.t: Heartland review – Jessica Chastain’s Netflix country music thriller is more miss than hit

items.title: Snoh Aalegra: Legendary Love review – raw R&B talent restrained by reverence for the greats
items.summary:
(Stem) 
Her truly remarkable, Sade-ish voice is hypnotic against some dizzyingly plush production, but a modern spin on 80s pastiche sometimes veers too close to tribute

Swedish-Iranian singer Snoh Aalegra has previously described her music – a lush, pastiche-y mix of R&B, hip-hop, soul and pop – as “cinematic soul”. But although she’s a dab hand at graceful, timeless presentation (and has a truly remarkable voice) Aalegra’s music has often struggled to match up to its aesthetic, hampered by her love of the greats and a penchant for broadly generic lyrics. Her most recent album, 2021’s Temporary Highs in the Violet Skies , made some headway toward carving out a more distinctive sound, thanks to sparky and inventive production from Tyler, the Creator, No ID, P2J and the Neptunes, but still didn’t quite feel like the right fit.

Aalegra’s fourth album is her most successful front-to-back statement yet, even if she can’t shake off the talent-show-ish reverence for her idols. Sparse and warm, Legendary Love puts her androgynous, Sade-ish voice in dizzyingly plush environments: a hybrid of Afrobeats and 80s R&B on the hypnotic I Love You ; a bed of minimalist guitars and moonlit synths on This That, which sounds as though it could have been produced by Jai Paul.

items.title: This Cursed Beautiful Land by Evan Gershkovich review – jailed in Putin’s Russia
items.summary:
The US reporter wrongly imprisoned for espionage writes compellingly about his ordeal

Evan Gershkovich is the Wall Street Journal reporter who, in the early phase of Putin’s war in Ukraine, was snatched up by the Russian authorities on bogus espionage charges and spent a year and a half in Russian jails (first Lefortovo and then Yekaterinburg) before being released in a prisoner exchange in 2024.

The opening section of his book about the experience is gripping and rather moving. He recounts his arrest in a sting operation, after meeting a contact who promised to supply him with information about Russia’s military-industrial preparations. Born to Russian Jewish immigrant parents in the US, Gershkovich grew up in suburban New Jersey on a diet of Soviet cartoons and “Krylov’s fables rather than Aesop’s”; he was betwixt and between. When he found his way into journalism in his early 20s – first working nights as an editorial assistant at the New York Times, then getting started properly as a reporter at the Moscow Times – he gravitated to Russia and fell in love with it.

A contortionist crawls out of a safety deposit box in the wall of an underground Swiss bank vault, legs wrapped around his waist, feet resting on his lumbar spine, landing on hands and displaced knees on the tiled floor. You know what? SOLD. You have just earned my undivided attention for the next hour of whatever you want to present to me.

Under such highly promising circumstances does the new heist thriller 12 12 12 begin. It stars Anthony Mackie of the Marvel Cinematic Universe and Jamie Dornan (building a nice career since 2013’s The Fall , if we gloss over the 50 Shades movies and the one where he played a romantic hero who believed he was a bee ) as its antagonists locked in an international cat-and-mouse game over eight episodes. items.title: Artnet’s Kalshi Partnership Faces Swift Backlash Online, But Advisers Are More Mixed
items.summary:
The art world, as much as we love it, has never been accused of lacking opportunities for speculation. But apparently “ there’s room for one more, honey. “

On Wednesday, Artnet announced that it had partnered with Kalshi, the prediction-market platform that lets users bet on everything from election results to sporting events. Artnet will become Kalshi’s official art partner, helping select markets and supplying the auction data used to determine which bets pay out.

The reaction on Instagram was swift and, let’s say, not particularly kind.

“How convenient. Now you can misunderstand art from anywhere,” wrote one commenter.

“Listen y’all there simply weren’t enough ways to artificially inflate an artist’s market and destroy their career before they turn 30,” wrote another.

Then came perhaps the most inspired comment, which may be a prediction of Artnet’s next move on the chessboard: “UFC x ARTNET! ARTNET JOE ROGAN.”

The partnership comes seven months after Artnet, the auction-data and media company, announced a merger with the online art brokerage Artsy. The combined company is led by chairman Andrew Wolff, CEO of Beowolff Capital, which acquired majority stakes in both companies over the past year.

It also comes just days before New York’s marquee November sales, which will offer plenty of chances to put the partnership to the test. Kalshi introduced art-related prediction markets in May and already offers contracts on individual paintings, entire collections, and whether artists will break their auction records.

Take Yoshitomo Nara’s Candy Blue Night (2001), which…
items.t: Artnet’s Kalshi Partnership Faces Swift Backlash Online, But Advisers Are More Mixed

items.title: The Good Daughter review – the best thing about this legal thriller? Brendan Gleeson’s sad toilet fart
items.summary:
For a drama that is meant to explore female trauma, Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy are given very little to do as small-town lawyers. It is Gleeson who steals the show as their broken father who earns the name Shatticus Finch

“Why is ma laaahf filled with contrary feee-males ?” grumbles dilapidated defence lawyer Rusty Quinn (Brendan Gleeson), his deep south vowels stretching like grilled cheese across his cluttered desk.

Poor Rusty. As the father of two headstrong lawyer daughters, this sunken beanbag of fading masculinity is forced daily to endure the contrariness of feee-males who are forever challengin’ the status quo. “This is all bullshit,” snaps elder daughter Sam (Rose Byrne), by way of illustration. “You’re a dipshit,” adds Charlie (Meghann Fahy), thoughtfully. They sure don’t make his laaahf easy! But the sisters love ol’ Rusty, or at least do their best to tolerate his excruciating aphorisms (“Never kick a fresh turd on a hot day,” etc), and when a school shooting forces them to confront a long-buried family tragedy, the Quinns pull together. They need each other. Dammit, the whole town needs them. After all, shouts Charlie, “We’re the only lawyers that don’t roll over for the local cops!” Thus begins The Good Daughter, a steaming hillock of “smalltown secrets” bunkum that fulfils precisely the same purpose as a Harlan Coben adaptation. 

The Good Daughter is on Sky Atlantic and Now in the UK, on Stan in Australia and on Peacock in the US

items.t: The Good Daughter review – the best thing about this legal thriller? Brendan Gleeson’s sad toilet fart

items.title: MoMA Shells Out $200,000 for Inaugural Ambasz Prize for ‘Nature-Reconciled’ Architecture, Half of Which Will Go To Plant Trees
items.summary:
As experts gather in Antalya, Turkey for the United Nations COP31 climate change conference, the nonprofit Climate Action Tracker is warning of devastating warming by 2100, and the EU reports that global warming has accelerated significantly since the 2015 Paris climate agreement, notes Inside Climate News .

Against this grim backdrop, New York’s Museum of Modern Art is announcing that it will give an annual grant totaling $200,000 in recognition of a single project by architects whose work is, as the award name has it, “nature-reconciled.” The prize comes with a $100,000 cash purse for the winner; it also includes another $100,000 that will go to a nonprofit organization to plant trees in the project client’s name. The prize is named the Ambasz-MoMA prize in return for a major gift from the Legacy Emilio Ambasz Foundation. It will recognize projects created anywhere in the world in the last three decades that “repair architecture’s relationship with nature,” as the museum puts it in press materials.

The museum bills it as the largest award for a single project in the field of architecture. The $100,000 cash component equals that of the Pritzker Architecture Prize, which honors living architects for significant achievement. The full $200,000 award equals the Driehaus Prize, given annually by the University of Notre Dame to a living architect working in traditional and classical architectural forms.

An Argentinian-American architect, Ambasz has had a longstanding relationship with the museum, having served as a curator in the architecture and design department between…
items.t: MoMA Shells Out $200,000 for Inaugural Ambasz Prize for ‘Nature-Reconciled’ Architecture, Half of Which Will Go To Plant Trees

items.title: Lorna Simpson Wins $105,000 Wolfgang Hahn Prize
items.summary:
American artist Lorna Simpson, who pioneered a new approach to conceptual photography, has been named the winner of the 2027 Wolfgang Hahn Prize. The Museum Ludwig in Cologne, Germany, which sponsors the annual prize, will put €100,000 (about $105,000) toward the acquisition of a work by Simpson for its collection. A solo exhibition of her work will staged by the institution next year, accompanied by a publication.

The 2027 award jury comprised Naomi Beckwith, deputy director and chief curator of the Guggenheim Museum in New York, and artistic director of documenta 16, and the Museum Ludwig board. 

Born in Brooklyn, Simpson rose to international renown in the 1990s with multilayered photographs that pair images with fragmented text. Her practice eventually expanded to encompass film, painting, drawing, and sculpture, often blending the boundaries between mediums while remaining focused on inner worlds and popular perceptions of Black women.

Her two-part photo-text work ID (1990) was included in Museum Ludwig’s 1999 group exhibition “Art Worlds in Dialogue (Kunstwelten im Dialog).” In that work, Simpson paired two portraits of a Black woman. In one, she turns her back to the camera; a plaque bearing the word “identity” is mounted alongside the image. The other reveals only the crown of her head, which resembles the Earth emerging from deep space. A plaque engraved with the word “identify” is mounted over this image. The museum’s catalog text from 1999 compared ID to the Black Madonna of Cologne, a famous wooden statute and site of pilgrimage housed in a 17th-century…
items.t: Lorna Simpson Wins $105,000 Wolfgang Hahn Prize

items.title: Monumental Equestrian Statue of Roman Emperor Once Stood in Second Century Scotland
items.summary:
Once part of a monumental Roman-era equestrian statue, a gilded bronze lower leg and foot found in a bog in Milsington, Scotland, in 1820 will be a highlight of a new show at the National Museum of Scotland in Edinburgh. The artifact, which dates to approximately 140 CE, was originally thought to have been looted by Scottish tribes from a site further south. But experts new believe that it came from a sculpture erected locally by Roman conquerors.

A study of sculpture fragments from Roman Scotland has shown that imperial statuary was a feature of Roman frontier forts, making a Scottish origin for the work more likely. In addition, a new analysis by National Museums Scotland shows the bronze limb was carefully detached from its parent statue, suggesting that the monument was deliberately dismantled rather than destroyed.

Archaeologists now think that the statue depicted the Roman Emperor Antonius Pius, who led Rome’s second major military campaign into Scotland. Under his leadership, Roman forces built the turf Antonine Wall across what is now Scotland’s Central Belt; attacks by Caledonian tribes forced a retreat south to Hadrian’s Wall less than a generation later.

“It offers us a tantalizing glimpse into the kind of grand monuments which once stood in southern Scotland and shows the importance Pius placed on his victories in Scotland,” Fraser Hunter, the principal curator of the upcoming exhibition, “Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire,” said of the remnant. “But it begs the question: Where is the rest of the statue?”

items.title: Vienna Actionism Museum to Cease Exhibition Program Following Controversial Otto Muehl Show
items.summary:
The Vienna Actionism Museum will end its exhibition program in 2027 and transition into a research institution dedicated to the transgressive postwar art movement, Monopol reports . The research institution will be open to the public by appointment only.

The privately owned institution has been a controversial presence in Austria’s art scene since opening in 2024, owing to its focus on a movement known for violent, visceral performances that often used blood and excrement as materials. But public discontent escalated into outrage earlier this year, after the museum announced that its fall exhibition would be dedicated to the work of prominent Actionist Otto Muehl , who was convicted in 1991 of crimes including the sexual abuse of minors living in a commune he led throughout the 1970s and ’80s. The show opened on September 10 and will be on view through January 10, 2027.

Muehl reentered the art scene with apparent ease after his release in 1997, receiving exhibitions at prominent Viennese institutions, including the Museum of Applied Arts, the Leopold Museum, and the gallery W&K – Wienerroither & Kohlbacher. His market surged after his death in 2014, with his works continuing to fetch six-figure prices at galleries and auction houses throughout the 2010s, according to the Artnet Price Database.

This year made clear that Muehl’s legacy was no longer so easily defended. The Vienna Actionism Museum’s exhibition, titled “ Otto Muehl: Art at the Abyss ,” reignited debate in Austria over the presentation of his work, particularly after several living survivors of the commune…
items.t: Vienna Actionism Museum to Cease Exhibition Program Following Controversial Otto Muehl Show

items.title: American Novelist and Four Others to Stand Trial Over Sale of Gold Looted from Shipwreck
items.summary:
In a story that sounds ripped from the pages of a novel, an American novelist, her husband, and three French nationals are set to stand trial in France next May for their alleged involvement in the resale of gold bars looted from an 18th-century shipwreck decades ago.

Eleanor “Gay” Courter, 82, an author of best-selling fiction, nonfiction, and memoir; her husband, Philip Courter, 84, a film director; Yves Gladu, 79, a professional underwater photographer; his wife, Brigitte Gladu, 76; and his sister-in-law, Annette May Pesty, 80, have all been charged with conspiracy. Some also face charges of money laundering and receiving stolen goods.

According to her website , Gay Courter has mainly written historical fiction and thrillers. And in case you were wondering, none of her books has a plot involving gold looted from a mysterious shipwreck.

The case will go before a criminal court in Brest on May 27, 2027, Agence France-Presse reported.

The case begins with the 1974 discovery of Le Prince de Conty , a French trading ship that sank off the coast of Brittany in 1746. The wreck was found 30 to 50 feet underwater near the island of Belle-Île-en-Mer. After gold bullion was discovered there, the site was looted in 1975. Lawsuits tied up the wreck until the mid-1980s, according to France’s Department of Underwater Archaeological Research (DRASSM). In 1985, archaeologists resumed excavations to the site and recovered Chinese porcelain dating to the 18th century, tea crates, and three ingots of Chinese gold. However that same year, a storm battered the ship and the wreck was…

items.title: Chicago’s Viral ‘Bean’ Stunt Inspires Londoners to Move the Marble Arch
items.summary:
Londoners want to get in on the viral stunt of the Bean, British Indian artist Anish Kapoor ’s silvery sculpture Cloud Gate (2006), by wanting to move the Marble Arch, designed by John Nash in 1827.

“Bean there, done that,” as Ocula reports, responding to a public listing on the platform Partiful planned for Saturday, inviting people to move the 19th-century white marble-faced triumphal arch 17.78 cm (7 inches) to the left, the same distance that Chicagoans recently tried to push Kapoor’s sculpture in the city’s Millennium Park. The Chicago stunt failed to work, primarily because the Bean, as the public artwork is nicknamed, weighs 110 tons.

The event description on Partiful said, “We have been made aware that the top floor of the marble arch [sic] was used for incarceration. People could still be trapped inside.” A representative of the artist Stuart Semple, who is known for disputing with Anish Kapoor in the past over questions like paint color, told Ocula that Londoners supported Chicago bean-pushers. The representative added that “planning to push the Arch to send a clear message that the bloke in the Bean must be freed” and that “moving the Arch will prove to Chicago that it’s possible, and will hopefully inspire them to try again to free the man.”

The Bean-pushing phenomenon has been all fun and games on social media. The Instagram account @Maninabean on Monday said that “as a coalition of non-violent like-minded individuals, we commend all action towards freeing the man.” The Instagram account was created in 2025 with its first published post on July 28, 2025…

items.title: ‘Joni Mitchell sang Both Sides, Now over the phone to me’: folk music legend Judy Collins on her 87 remarkable years

As she continues her farewell tour, the US singer-songwriter answers your questions on romance with Stephen Stills, friendship with Carly Simon and how folk underpins all pop

How did you come into Joni Mitchell ’s orbit and how did you end up recording Both Sides, Now before she did? Steve-bayley

I’m 48 years sober, but in the old days I drank. One night in 1967, I was passed out and the phone rang at about 3am. It was my friend [the musician, songwriter and producer] Al Kooper. He said he’d been at a club and had run into this woman, Joni, who wrote songs. He put her on the phone and she sang Both Sides, Now over the phone. It was brilliant. I said: “I’ll be right over.” I recorded it the next day and it became a huge hit.

I don’t think Joni was too happy that I was the first to record it, but she was very generous and I’ve since recorded many of her songs. She was unknown then, so I’m proud that I was able to help introduce her to the world. She’s one of the great writers of all time.

items.title: ‘To them, we’re just NPCs’: the artists and activists challenging Trump’s video game propaganda
items.summary:
Order a Diet Coke or invade Iran – that’s the choice facing the US president in one of several satirical games, as designers turn the gamification of politics back on the White House

In early September, the Trump White House announced a surprising new addition to its official website. Named simply Arcade , it is a collection of browser games based on classic titles such as Flappy Bird, Snake, and Tetris, but re-tuned as flagrant works of political propaganda. Designed to court reactionary gamers, they push the administration’s policies on immigration and other hot-button issues, while dehumanising their targets. There have recently been some new additions: a Temple Run clone named Red Scare about crossing the “ration market” and escaping the Democratic Socialists of America, and another simple item-matching game about the threat of socialism. In the midst of increasing fuel, utility and grocery prices thanks to the Iran war, these were naked attempts to distract voters by appealing to their video game nostalgia.

After an explosion of news coverage, Arcade caught the attention of the games industry. The Tetris Company warned on social media that it “took copyright infringement very seriously.” Days later, the game was removed from the White House site. However, aside from a March 2026 statement from the Pokémon Company condemning the White House for using its characters in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) propaganda, major video game companies have been relatively silent in the face of the administration’s widespread usage of their IP.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘To them, we’re just NPCs’: the artists and activists challenging Trump’s video game propaganda

The It Follows and Longlegs star tears into the role of a murderous governess in this hit-and-miss adaptation of Virginia Feito’s gory novel

It’s not that hard to figure out why a lower-class woman toiling away in Victorian England would be so easily driven to violently murder everyone around her. If it’s not the brittle entitlement of those who employ you, it’s the unending misogyny of the system you’re forced to be a subservient part of, all the while being underpaid and undervalued and at the mercy of sexual violence, a multitude of diseases and an average lifespan of just 42.

As Winifred Notty (Maika Monroe) fills the frame in Victorian Psycho, heading to a new job as governess for a rich family, it’s easy to be on her side. Even as her murderous impulses start to rear their head, they’re made somewhat understandable, although Winifred isn’t just a woman reacting to the various injustices of the time – she’s one responding to a demon within her, a darkness she has chosen to embrace rather than resist. Darkness is her friend, a protection against harm, and a way to possess some sort of control in a world that has denied her any of it.

items.title: 2,800-Year-Old Bone Flute Unearthed in Troy May Have Been Played During Homer’s Time
items.summary:
Image by Mehmet Nuri Ersoy, via Twitter 

The prolific Hans Zimmer scored Christopher Nolan’s films over the dozen years from Batman Begins through Dunkirk . From 2020’s Tenet onward, Nolan has employed the younger Swedish composer Ludwig Göransson . Just what difference this has made in the resulting pictures is a matter best left to the scrutiny of the most obsessive fans, but any viewer can hear how much Zimmer and Göransson differ stylistically. This past summer, the siren song included on the soundtrack of The Odyssey featured one of the latter’s particularly notable choices: the use of an aulos, a double-reeded wind instrument much played back in ancient Greece.

Though Göransson didn’t have a genuinely ancient aulos on hand, of course, the sound produced by the replica proved evocative enough. But just this year, as it happens, a bone flute actually dating from the period in which Homer wrote The Odyssey was unearthed from the archaeological site of ancient Troy in modern-day northwestern Turkey.

As Smithsonian.com’s Meilan Solly writes , the past 160 years of digging there have produced “a pair of gold diadems, more than 100 two-handled wine goblets, and arrowheads and weapons dated to the Late Bronze Age, among other artifacts.” This 2,800-year-old flute isn’t just the first musical instrument discovered at the site, but also further evidence that Troy wasn’t the ghost town it was once assumed to be in the eighth century BC.

As always when dealing with ancient artifacts — and especially ones, as these pictures reveal, in a less-than-whole state — we should be…
items.t: 2,800-Year-Old Bone Flute Unearthed in Troy May Have Been Played During Homer’s Time

items.title: When Salvador Dali Met Sigmund Freud, and Changed Freud’s Mind About Surrealism (1938)
items.summary:
The close associations between Surrealism and Freudian psychoanalysis were liberally encouraged by the most famous proponent of the movement, Salvador Dalí, who considered himself a devoted follower of Freud. We don’t have to wonder what the founder of psychoanalysis would have thought of his self-appointed protégé.

We have them recording, in their own words, their impressions of their one and only meeting—which took place in July of 1938, at Freud’s home in London. Freud was 82, Dalí 34. We also have sketches Dalí made of Freud while the two sat together. Their memories of events, shall we say, differ considerably, or at least they seemed totally bewildered by each other. (Freud pronounced Dalí a “fanatic.”)

In any case, there’s absolutely no way the encounter could have lived up to Dalí’s expectations, as the Freud Museum London notes :

[Dalí] had already travelled to Vienna several times but failed to make an introduction. Instead, he wrote in his autobiography, he spent his time having “long and exhaustive imaginary conversations” with his hero, at one point fantasizing that he “came home with me and stayed all night clinging to the curtains of my room in the Hotel Sacher.” 

Freud was certainly not going to indulge Dalí’s peculiar fantasies, but what the artist really wanted was validation of his work—and maybe his very being. “Dalí had spent his teens and early twenties reading Freud’s works on the unconscious,” writes Paul Gallagher at Dangerous Minds , “on sexuality and The Interpretation of Dreams .” He was obsessed. Finally meeting Freud in ’38, he must have…
items.t: When Salvador Dali Met Sigmund Freud, and Changed Freud’s Mind About Surrealism (1938)

items.title: Watch Seoul’s 6,500-Year Evolution in a Mesmerizing 3D Animated Time Lapse
items.summary:
In this century, few countries have been as visibly successful as South Korea. China’s vertiginous economic rise once absorbed vast amounts of news-media attention, but its soft power has comparatively little reach across the wider world, at least in English-speaking countries. By this point, many if not most Westerners haven’t just eaten Korean food, but also driven a Korean car, heard Korean pop music, or watched a Korean film or TV show. The resulting sense of familiarity can prove deceptive to those who eventually make the trip there, but it does, at least, mark an improvement on the scant knowledge of the place they had before. Not so long ago, they could say little with certainty except this: South Korea’s got Seoul.

I first saw that pun on a T‑shirt in high school, long before I knew much of anything about Korea myself. Now, having lived there for more than a decade, I’ve been able to watch from the inside as the country’s capital has become an unlikely object of general interest. As evidence, take the 1.2 million views already racked up by the new video from Latos Charts above, a 3D animated time lapse showing the evolution of Seoul over six and a half often tumultuous millennia.

It reveals, among other things, that the city didn’t exist for most of the history of Korean civilization — but then, neither did the country. The postwar division of the peninsula into North and South has a kind of precedent in the warring kingdoms that occupied it before its unification by a series of states culminating in the 500-year rule of the Joseon Dynasty.

If you’ve watched one…

items.title: Inspiration from Charles Bukowski: You Might Be Old, Your Life May Be “Crappy,” But You Can Still Make Good Art

Now more than ever, there’s tremendous pressure to make it big while you’re young.

Pity the 31-year-old who fails to make it onto a 30-under-30 list…

The soon-to-graduate high schooler passed over for YouTube stardom…

The great hordes who creep into middle age without so much as a TED Talk to their names…

Social media definitely magnifies the sensation that an unacceptable number of our peers have been granted first-class cabins aboard a ship that’s sailed without us. If we weren’t so demoralized, we’d sue Instagram for creating the impression that everyone else’s perfectly filtered life is leading to book deals and profiles in The New Yorker .

Don’t despair, dear reader. Charles Bukowski is about to make your day from beyond the grave.

In 1993, at the age of 73, the late writer and self-described “spoiled old toad,” took a break from recording the audiobook of Run With the Hunted to reflect upon his “crappy” life.

Some of these thoughts made it into Drew Christie’s animation, above, a reminder that the smoothest road isn’t always necessarily the richest one.

In service of his ill-paying muse, Bukowski logged decades in unglamorous jobs—dishwasher, truck driver and loader, gas station attendant, stock boy, warehouseman, shipping clerk, parking lot attendant, Red Cross orderly, elevator operator, and most notoriously, postal carrier and clerk. These gigs gave him plenty of material, the sort of real world experience that eludes those upon whom literary fame and fortune smiles early.

items.title: The Painting Nobody Wanted: How Matisse’s The Red Studio Went from a London Nightclub to a Masterpiece of Modern Art
items.summary:
A journalist paid Henri Matisse a visit not long after he’d painted The Red Studio in 1911. “I like it, but I don’t completely understand it,” the artist is quoted as admitting of that latest work. “I like it, but I don’t know why I precisely painted it this way.” The painting was a rendition of the very same Issy-les-Moulineaux studio in which they were talking, though you wouldn’t necessarily recognize it at first glance. Deep red covered two-thirds of its surface, an unorthodox choice that probably contributed to its rejection by Matisse’s loyal patron Sergei Shchukin, who’d commissioned Dance and Music . This departure from strict representation fared no better when it was shown in London, and thereafter at the groundbreaking 1913 “Armory Show” in the United States.

By 1926, when The Red Studio finally made its Paris debut, public sensibilities had begun to catch up with Matisse’s instincts. The following year, it found a buyer in the owner of London’s Gargoyle Club, a favorite haunt of the Bright Young Things, where the painting would hang for more than a decade.

Eventually it ended up at the Museum of Modern Art , whose video at the top of the post tells the story of the painting’s journey from enduring absolute rejection to exerting great influence on postwar New York artists like Mark Rothko, Barnett Newman, and Ellsworth Kelly. All of those younger painters were exploring the possibilities of what MoMA curator Ann Temkin calls “a big expanse of color that doesn’t describe anything, that just is there for its own expressive purposes.”

Gallerist-YouTuber James…

items.title: When Charles Dickens Met Edgar Allan Poe
items.summary:
“There comes Poe with his raven,” wrote the poet James Russell Lowell in 1848, “like Barnaby Rudge, / Three-fifths of him genius and two-fifths sheer fudge.” Barnaby Rudge , as you may know, is a novel by Charles Dickens , published serially in 1841. Set during the anti-Catholic Gordon Riots of 1780, the book stands as Dickens’ first historical novel and a prelude of sorts to A Tale of Two Cities . But what, you may wonder, does it have to do with Poe and “his raven”?

Quite a lot, it turns out. Poe reviewed the first four chapters of Dickens’ Barnaby Rudge for Graham’s Magazine , predicting the end of the novel and finding out later he was correct when he reviewed it again upon completion. He was particularly taken with one character: a chatty raven named Grip who accompanies the simple-minded Barnaby. Poe described the bird as “intensely amusing,” points out Atlas Obscura , and also wrote that Grip’s “croaking might have been prophetically heard in the course of the drama.”

It chanced the following year the two literary greats would meet, when Poe learned of Dickens’ trip to the U.S.; he wrote to the novelist, and the two briefly exchanged letters (which you can read here ). Along with Dickens on his six-month journey were his wife Catherine, his children, and Grip, his pet raven. When the two writers met in person, writes Lucinda Hawksley at the BBC, Poe “was enchanted to discover [Grip, the character] was based on Dickens’s own bird.”

Indeed Dickens’ raven, “who had an impressive vocabulary,” inspired what Dickens called the “very queer character” in Barnaby Rudge ,…
items.t: When Charles Dickens Met Edgar Allan Poe

items.title: Explore the Reading List for Harvard’s Humanities 10: The “Brutal” Humanities Class That’s Suddenly in High Demand

There are plenty of good reasons a student might want to go to Harvard. One is its long history, at least by American standards; another is the formidable accomplishments of the professors hired to teach there. But on some level, a teenager looking to come up in the world — or, in many cases, parents looking to put their teenager up in the world — understands full well that much of what an institution like Harvard offers comes down to its selectivity. Considering how few get in versus how many apply, it would be easy to believe that most of a student’s battle is won at the point of acceptance. Imagine the despair, then, of a newly arrived Harvardian facing another entrance exam and written application just to get a seat in Humanities 10 .

Its unintimidating name notwithstanding, Humanities 10 is the opposite of one of those introductory courses through which a vast, darkened lecture hall full of freshmen can doze. “Students read a hefty book a week and write regular essays,” reports Pamela Paul in a recent Wall Street Journal article. “There is no pass/fail option. Digital devices are verboten, and attendance is taken in every lecture.” This year’s syllabus, which the WSJ has also published (also find it below), “begins with The Odyssey , travels forward in time to James Joyce’s Ulysses and then backward to end with The Iliad . In between are assignments on Montaigne, Shakespeare, Spinoza, Baldwin, Dante and Plato.” Amid these great books of the Western world appear works by Lady Murasaki, Sor Juana, and Cao Xueqin. 

With certain exceptions — Baldwin’s essays, three…
items.t: Explore the Reading List for Harvard’s Humanities 10: The “Brutal” Humanities Class That’s Suddenly in High Demand

items.title: “Don’t Try”: Charles Bukowski’s Concise Philosophy of Art and Life
items.summary:
In 1994, Charles Bukowski was buried in a Los Angeles cemetery, beneath a simple gravestone. The stone memorializes the poet’s name. It recites his dates of birth and death, but adds the symbol of a boxer between the two, suggesting his life was a struggle. And it adds the very succinct epitaph, “Don’t Try.”

There you have it, Bukowski’s philosophy on art and life boiled down to two words. But what do they mean? Let’s look back at the epistolary record and find out.

In October 1963, Bukowski recounted in a letter to John William Corrington how someone once asked him, “What do you do? How do you write, create?” To which, he replied: “You don’t try. That’s very important: ‘not’ to try, either for Cadillacs, creation or immortality. You wait, and if nothing happens, you wait some more. It’s like a bug high on the wall. You wait for it to come to you. When it gets close enough you reach out, slap out and kill it. Or if you like its looks you make a pet out of it.”

So, the key to life and art, it’s all about persistence? Patience? Timing? Waiting for your moment? Yes, but not just that.

Jumping forward to 1990, Bukowski sent a letter to his friend William Packard and reminded him: “We work too hard. We try too hard. Don’t try. Don’t work. It’s there. It’s been looking right at us, aching to kick out of the closed womb. There’s been too much direction. It’s all free, we needn’t be told. Classes? Classes are for asses. Writing a poem is as easy as beating your meat or drinking a bottle of beer.”

The key to living a good life, to creating great art — it’s also about not…
items.t: “Don’t Try”: Charles Bukowski’s Concise Philosophy of Art and Life
